items.title: Mitral stenosis – management (medical, PBMV, repair, replacement) & haemodynamic goals
items.summary: Medical therapy in mitral stenosis (MS) controls symptoms, rate and clot risk but does not fix the valve. Once MS is significant (MVA ≤1.5 cm²) and the patient has symptoms, the valve needs mechanical relief. Balloon valvotomy (PBMV/PMC) is first choice when anatomy is favourable; surgery is for those unsuitable for, or failed by, PBMV. Within surgery, a valve-sparing repair/open commissurotomy is preferred if the valve is pliable enough; replacement (MVR) is for valves too calcified, fibrosed or regurgitant to repair.

rows: MVA ≤1.5 cm² (very severe ≤1.0); mean gradient usually >5–10 mmHg at normal HR; PASP often >50
Mobility, leaflet thickening, subvalvular thickening, calcification, each 1–4 (total 4–16). ≤8 favourable for PBMV

sections.h: Medical management (all patients; bridge, not cure)
items: Rate control – β-blocker first, or non-DHP CCB (verapamil/diltiazem); digoxin if AF with LV dysfunction. Longer diastole = more LV filling, lower LA pressure
Diuretics (loop) + salt restriction for pulmonary congestion; avoid over-drying (preload-dependent)

Anticoagulation with warfarin (VKA, INR 2–3) if AF, prior embolism or LA thrombus; consider with very large LA or dense spontaneous echo contrast. DOACs NOT used in moderate–severe rheumatic MS (INVICTUS trial)
AF: rate control ± cardioversion/rhythm control after intervention; anticoagulate before cardioversion
Secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever – benzathine penicillin G 1.2 MU IM every 3–4 weeks (long-term; duration by age/carditis)
Infective endocarditis prophylaxis/dental hygiene, treat anaemia/infection, avoid tachycardia, counsel about pregnancy (treat severe MS before conception)
Asymptomatic mild–moderate MS: medical therapy + echo follow-up (severe yearly, moderate 1–2 yearly)
Symptomatic (NYHA II–IV) + MVA ≤1.5 cm² → intervene (PBMV if suitable, else surgery)

Asymptomatic severe MS → consider PBMV (if favourable anatomy, low risk) when: PASP >50 mmHg at rest, new AF, high embolic risk (prior embolism, dense LA contrast), planned pregnancy or major non-cardiac surgery
Symptoms but MVA >1.5 cm²: exercise echo – PBMV considered if gradient/PASP rises a lot on exercise (mean gradient >15, PASP >60)
Already having other cardiac surgery (CABG/AVR) + severe MS → do mitral surgery at the same time

rows: Pliable, non-calcified leaflets, Wilkins ≤8, commissural fusion present, MR ≤ mild (grade ≤2/4), no LA/LAA thrombus on TEE, young patient, sinus rhythm

LA or LAA thrombus (on TEE – do TEE before every PBMV); moderate–severe MR; MVA >1.5 cm²; severe or bicommissural calcification; no commissural fusion; severe aortic valve disease or severe TR/TS needing surgery; CAD needing CABG
Wilkins >8 but not heavily calcified, elderly, high surgical risk/pregnant → PBMV still reasonable (good result in ~40% of score >8)
Warfarin 1–3 months, repeat TEE; if resolved → PBMV, if not → surgery
MVA ≥1.5 cm² with ≤ mild MR increase; main complication = severe MR (needs urgent MVR), tamponade, embolism, residual ASD

Symptomatic severe MS (NYHA III–IV) and: not a PBMV candidate (anatomy/contraindication), failed or restenosed after PBMV, LA thrombus persisting despite anticoagulation, ≥moderate MR, concomitant cardiac surgery, or no PBMV expertise
Beating heart, no bypass, finger/Tubbs dilator via LA appendage. Same anatomy as PBMV; used in low-resource settings / pregnancy. Mostly replaced by PBMV

On bypass under direct vision: incise fused commissures, split fused chordae/papillary muscles, remove thrombus, ± annuloplasty and LAA excision. Choose when leaflets still reasonably pliable, little calcium, MR mild–moderate and repairable, or LA thrombus present but valve otherwise good. Better than PBMV when Wilkins >8 with some pliability

Keeps native valve and subvalvular apparatus (LV function), no lifelong anticoagulation (if sinus), lower thromboembolism/bleeding. Needs ongoing penicillin prophylaxis; restenosis/reoperation possible

When repair not possible: heavy leaflet/annular calcification, severe subvalvular fusion and shortening (thick, matted chordae), rigid immobile leaflets, severe/mixed MR not repairable, failed prior repair/PBMV, restenosis with unfavourable anatomy. Preserve chordae where possible

Mechanical: younger (<50 ACC/AHA, <65 ESC for mitral), already on warfarin for AF, can do INR – target INR 2.5–3.5. Bioprosthetic: older (>65–70), high bleeding risk, poor INR access, woman wanting pregnancy (discussed)

sections.h: Why preload matters so much (haemodynamics / anaesthesia)
items: The LV itself usually contracts normally – the problem is underfilling. Flow from LA to LV across the narrow valve depends on the LA–LV pressure gradient and on how long diastole lasts
Preload (venous return → LA pressure) is what keeps that gradient up; if preload falls the gradient collapses and stroke volume drops – a relatively 'fixed cardiac output' state
Normal hearts offset low filling with a faster HR; in MS tachycardia shortens diastole and reduces filling further – hypovolaemia + reflex tachycardia is the classic crash
Atrial kick contributes a larger share of LV filling across a stenotic valve; new AF (common, big LA) removes it and usually comes with a fast rate → sudden decompensation
Narrow window: LA pressure already near the pulmonary oedema threshold, so too little fluid = hypotension/low output, too much = pulmonary oedema (worse with pulmonary hypertension and a strained RV)
PCWP reflects LA pressure, not LVEDP – it overestimates LV filling in MS
Watch for preload drops: spinal/epidural sympatholysis (titrate slowly, epidural preferred over single-shot spinal), blood loss, aggressive diuresis, head-up position, positive pressure ventilation

Targets: euvolaemia, HR ~60–80 (treat tachycardia with β-blocker/esmolol), sinus rhythm (cardiovert unstable AF), maintain SVR (phenylephrine), avoid PVR rise (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, pain, N2O)

Algorithm: significant MS → symptoms? → PBMV-suitable anatomy (Wilkins ≤8, MR ≤ mild, no LA clot)? → PBMV; if not → surgery → repair/open commissurotomy if valve pliable, MVR if calcified/fibrosed/regurgitant
Always TEE before PBMV to exclude LA appendage clot
Medical therapy does not change natural history – only relieves symptoms and prevents embolism
Warfarin, not DOAC, for AF in rheumatic MS
Pregnancy with severe symptomatic MS refractory to drugs → PBMV in 2nd trimester is preferred over surgery
Anaesthesia goals: slow HR, sinus rhythm, adequate preload but no fluid overload, maintain SVR, avoid rise in PVR (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, pain)
Preload in MS = keeps the LA–LV gradient; slow HR = gives that gradient time to fill the LV. Both needed, because the LV cannot compensate by beating faster

items.pearl: Pliable + no clot + no MR → balloon; pliable but unsuitable for balloon → repair; calcified/fibrosed/regurgitant → replace.

items.title: ASA physical status
items.pearl: Grade = clinical judgement; the examples are guides, not rules.

refs.title: ASA Physical Status Classification System (ASA; last amended 13 Dec 2020, first approved 15 Oct 2014)
Günaydın B. ASA Physical Status Classification System. Turk J Anaesthesiol Reanim 2021;49:192–3
Parenti N et al. Reliability of ASA physical status classification. Indian J Anaesth 2016;60:208–14
Riley R et al. Inter-rater reliability of the ASA physical status classification. Anaesth Intensive Care 2014;42:614–8
SPA: Updated ASA physical status classification with paediatric examples

items.summary: The ASA Physical Status (ASA-PS) classification grades a patient's overall health before anaesthesia. Current version: amended by the ASA House of Delegates on 13 Dec 2020 (first approved in this form on 15 Oct 2014). The class definitions did not change in 2020; the update added adult, paediatric and obstetric examples.

rows: Normal healthy patient: no systemic disease, non-smoker, little or no alcohol.
Mild systemic disease without real functional limitation, e.g. current smoker, social drinker, normal pregnancy, BMI 30–40, well-controlled diabetes or hypertension, mild lung disease.

Severe systemic disease with functional limitation, e.g. poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, COPD, BMI 40 or more, active hepatitis, alcohol dependence, implanted pacemaker, moderately reduced ejection fraction, end-stage renal disease on regular dialysis, MI/stroke/TIA/coronary stent more than 3 months ago.

Severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life, e.g. MI/stroke/TIA/coronary stent within the last 3 months, ongoing cardiac ischaemia or severe valve disease, severely reduced ejection fraction, sepsis, DIC, ARDS, end-stage renal disease not on regular dialysis.

Moribund: not expected to survive without the operation, e.g. ruptured abdominal or thoracic aneurysm, massive trauma, intracranial bleed with mass effect, ischaemic bowel with multiple organ failure.
Declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donation.
Added to the class for an emergency operation: one where delay would significantly increase the threat to life or to a body part (e.g. ASA IIIE). Not used with ASA VI.

items: Normal pregnancy is ASA II (not ASA I).
Moves up a class as pregnancy complications become severe: e.g. pre-eclampsia with severe features is ASA III, and the same with HELLP or decompensated heart disease is ASA IV.
Uterine rupture is given as an ASA V example.
Add E when the case is an emergency (e.g. category 1 caesarean: ASA IIE or higher).
The 2020 update added a separate column of children's examples, which improved agreement between paediatric anaesthetists.

Typical pattern: well-controlled chronic conditions (asthma without exacerbation, controlled epilepsy) are ASA II; poorly controlled disease, ex-premature infants under 60 weeks postconceptional age and difficult airway are ASA III; symptomatic heart disease, sepsis or ventilator dependence are ASA IV.
See the ASA page (reference 1) for the full table of children's examples.
The examples are illustrative, not exhaustive; the ASA gives no further rules, so the final grade is the anaesthetist's clinical judgement.
ASA-PS describes the patient's health, not the risk of the operation itself: it does not include the type of surgery, age alone, or airway difficulty in adults.
Inter-rater agreement is only fair to moderate (kappa about 0.4 to 0.6 in most studies); ASA II and III are the classes most often disputed. Using the official examples improves agreement.
Despite this, higher ASA class is consistently linked with more postoperative complications and mortality, and ASA-PS is built into many risk scores (e.g. POSSUM-type models, NSQIP calculator).
In India, SLCM and most hospital PAC forms record ASA with the E suffix for emergencies.

items.title: Pressure support ventilation (PSV)
items.pearl: Used for weaning and SBT (e.g. PS 5–8 cmH2O + PEEP 5).

refs.title: Abramovitz A, Sung S. Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV). StatPearls. Treasure Island (FL): StatPearls Publishing; 2023 (archived)

Liberation from mechanical ventilation in critically ill adults: an official American College of Chest Physicians / American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline. Chest 2017 (suggests the first spontaneous breathing trial uses 5–8 cmH₂O of pressure support)
GE Aisys CS2 User's Reference Manual: ventilation modes, factory default settings (ManualsLib)

items.summary: Pressure support ventilation is a purely spontaneous mode: every breath is triggered by the patient, pressure-limited (the ventilator holds PEEP + PS) and flow-cycled (it stops when flow falls to a set percentage of peak flow). There is no set rate, so the patient needs an intact respiratory drive, and minute ventilation is not guaranteed.

items: Trigger: the patient's effort is sensed as a small fall in airway pressure or a change in flow.
The ventilator raises airway pressure to PEEP + PS and holds it there for the rest of inspiration.
Flow is highest at the start, then falls as the lungs fill.
Cycle: when flow falls to the set percentage of peak flow (commonly 25%), the ventilator stops and expiration begins.
The patient decides the rate and the inspiratory time. Tidal volume depends on the PS level, the patient's effort, compliance and resistance.

rows: Pressure added above PEEP. Usually 5–20 cmH₂O (the GE Aisys CS2 manual lists a range of 2–40). Titrate to a tidal volume of about 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, a rate under 25–30 and no accessory muscle use. A level of 5–8 cmH₂O roughly offsets the resistance of the tube and circuit, and is the level suggested for a spontaneous breathing trial.
Typically 5 cmH₂O. In COPD with intrinsic PEEP, external PEEP set below the intrinsic level reduces the effort needed to trigger a breath.
Set to reach the target SpO₂.

Flow trigger about 1–3 L/min, or pressure trigger about −0.5 to −2 cmH₂O. Too sensitive causes auto-triggering (leaks, cardiac oscillations, water in the circuit). Too insensitive causes missed efforts and extra work.

How fast the airway pressure reaches the target. Shown in seconds, as a percentage or on a 1–10 scale, depending on the ventilator. Use a faster rise for a patient with high drive. Too fast gives pressure overshoot and early cycling; too slow starves the patient of flow.
Expiratory trigger (Esens, cycle-off, End of breath)

The percentage of peak flow at which inspiration ends. Commonly 25% by default; the GE Aisys CS2 lists 5–75%. Raise it to about 40–50% in COPD to shorten inspiration and limit air trapping. Lower it to about 10–15% in stiff (restrictive) lungs to avoid cycling too early and double triggering.

A backup time limit on the breath, which matters with leaks and NIV. The value and name vary with the ventilator. Many ventilators also end the breath if pressure rises above the target (the patient breathing out against the breath).
If the patient does not breathe for the set apnoea time, a mandatory backup mode with a set rate takes over. The time varies by machine (the GE Aisys CS2 manual lists 10–30 s).
High and low respiratory rate, low and high minute volume and tidal volume, high airway pressure.
Optional on some ventilators. Adds extra pressure to offset the resistance of the tube.

sections.alt: Airway pressure and flow over one pressure support breath, marking the trigger, rise time, PEEP, PS, peak flow, the point where flow falls to about 25% of peak and the breath cycles off, and the inspiratory time.
items: Trigger: the small dip below PEEP, with the matching flow change, is the patient's effort being sensed.
Rise time: the slope from PEEP up to the plateau.
PS: the height of the plateau above PEEP. It is the main determinant of tidal volume.
Expiratory trigger: the flow tails off, and the breath ends when flow falls to the set percentage of peak. A higher setting ends the breath earlier; a lower setting ends it later.
Inspiratory time: the width of the plateau. It is not set. It comes from the patient's effort, the lung mechanics and the cycle-off point (plus the maximum inspiratory time backup).
Bedside check: if the flow curve ends abruptly instead of tapering, the breath cycled too early or too late, so adjust the expiratory trigger or the rise time.
Tidal volume is not fixed: it falls if compliance falls or resistance rises.
Too much support causes large volumes, hyperinflation, missed triggers and central apnoeas in sleep.
Too little support causes rapid shallow breathing and fatigue.
Sedation, opioids or residual neuromuscular block can cause hypoventilation. Because no mandatory breaths are given, minute ventilation is not guaranteed, which is why the apnoea backup matters.

Many anaesthesia machines offer pressure support with an apnoea backup, for example PSVPro on GE machines. If the patient stops breathing for the set backup time, a mandatory mode takes over. This is useful during emergence and LMA cases.
Names, ranges and defaults differ between machines, so check the manual of the machine you are using.

items.title: Paediatric spinal anaesthesia: dose
items.pearl: Smaller child = more mg/kg (more CSF per kg) but a shorter block.

refs.title: Gupta A, Saha U. Spinal anesthesia in children: a review. J Anaesthesiol Clin Pharmacol 2014;30:10–18
Greaney D, Everett T. Paediatric regional anaesthesia: updates in central neuraxial techniques and thoracic and abdominal blocks. BJA Educ 2019;19:126–34
Spinal anesthesia in infants and children: a one year prospective audit. Anesth Essays Res 2014;8:324–9

items.summary: The spinal dose in children is chosen by body weight, and the mg/kg dose rises as the child gets smaller. Infants have more CSF per kg, more of it in the spinal canal, and faster drug removal, so they need a larger weight-based dose and still get a shorter block than adults.

rows: 0.5 mg/kg (0.1 mL/kg) in some schemes; up to 1 mg/kg (0.2 mL/kg) in others, especially for awake neonatal and infant spinals.
Dose moves towards adult dosing; never give more than the adult dose.

sections.h: Why smaller children need more per kg
items: CSF volume per kg is higher: about 10 mL/kg in neonates and 4 mL/kg in infants and toddlers, against 2 mL/kg in adults.
About half of the CSF lies in the spinal canal in children, against roughly a third in adults, so the drug is diluted more.
A very vascular pia and a high cardiac output clear the drug quickly, so the block is short: about 45–90 minutes in neonates and infants.
The surgery: its expected length and the level of block needed.
Adjuvants to lengthen the block: clonidine 1 microgram/kg, fentanyl 0.2 microgram/kg (higher doses are also described), adrenaline 2–4 micrograms/kg.
Intrathecal morphine has been used, but only with monitored postoperative care.
Ex-premature infants (under 60 weeks postconceptional age): avoid sedatives and opioids where possible because of postoperative apnoea.
Volumes are tiny: draw up in a 1 mL syringe and allow for the dead space of the needle.
Puncture at L4–5 or L5–S1. At birth the cord ends near L3 and the dural sac at S3–S4; adult levels are reached by about 1–2 years.
Do not lift the legs after injection (for example to place the cautery pad): it can cause a high spinal.
Blood pressure usually stays stable in younger children (under about 5 years), so fluid preloading is not needed.
Dosing schemes differ slightly between texts: follow the department protocol.

items.title: Achalasia cardia
items.summary: Achalasia is a motility disorder in which the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) fails to relax on swallowing and the oesophageal body loses peristalsis, because the inhibitory nerves of the myenteric plexus degenerate. Food and fluid pool in a dilated oesophagus above a closed sphincter. For the anaesthetist the key issue is a large, retained oesophageal reservoir that can be regurgitated and aspirated at induction, regardless of fasting time.

items: Loss of inhibitory neurons (nitric oxide / VIP) in the myenteric plexus
LES has high resting tone and does not relax with swallowing
Absent peristalsis in the oesophageal body, so emptying depends on gravity
Mostly idiopathic; secondary form in Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) and pseudoachalasia from tumour at the cardia
Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the start (unlike stricture or cancer, which begin with solids)
Regurgitation of undigested food, often at night; chest pain; weight loss
Nocturnal cough or recurrent chest infections from silent aspiration
Barium swallow: dilated oesophagus tapering to a smooth 'bird's beak'
High-resolution manometry is the gold standard; endoscopy to exclude malignancy

rows: Classic: no pressurisation, minimal contractility; dilated oesophagus
Pan-oesophageal pressurisation; best response to treatment
Spastic, premature contractions; responds best to POEM (long myotomy)
Nifedipine or nitrates before meals; weak, short-lived effect
Endoscopic LES injection; for frail patients, lasts months
Balloon stretch of LES; small perforation risk
Per-oral endoscopic myotomy through a submucosal tunnel under GA

items: Treat as full stomach whatever the fasting time: the oesophagus holds retained food and fluid
Pre-op: liquid diet 24-48 h before, then clear fluids; ask about regurgitation and lying flat
Assess for aspiration lung disease, malnutrition, dehydration and electrolyte upset
Consider emptying the oesophagus before induction (wide-bore NG suction, or endoscopic clearance)
Head-up position; rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure (its value is debated with a dilated oesophagus)
Some centres prefer awake or head-up induction for a massively dilated oesophagus
Extubate fully awake with reflexes back, head-up
Antacid/H2 blocker premedication does little for oesophageal contents, which are not acidic stomach juice
GA with ETT and controlled ventilation; CO2 insufflation is used
CO2 can track out: subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, capnoperitoneum, capnothorax
Watch for rising EtCO2 and peak airway pressure, falling SpO2, abdominal distension
Decompress capnoperitoneum with a Veress needle; tension capnothorax needs a chest drain
Increase minute ventilation to clear the CO2 load; check for subcutaneous crepitus at end of case
Mucosal perforation and bleeding are surgical risks; plan for post-op nil by mouth and antiemetics
Achalasia = failed LES relaxation + aperistalsis; dysphagia to solids and liquids together
Bird's beak on barium; manometry confirms; Chicago types I-III
Main danger is aspiration of the oesophageal reservoir at induction, even after fasting
Empty the oesophagus, head-up, RSI, awake extubation
POEM: think CO2 complications (capnothorax, pneumoperitoneum, surgical emphysema)
Long-standing achalasia increases risk of squamous cell carcinoma of oesophagus

items.pearl: Fasting does not empty an achalasia oesophagus: suction it, sit them up, and do an RSI.

Vaezi MF et al. ACG Clinical Guidelines: Diagnosis and Management of Achalasia. Am J Gastroenterol 2020

items.title: CKD classification (KDIGO)
items.summary: Chronic kidney disease means kidney structure or function has been abnormal for more than 3 months, with consequences for health. KDIGO stages it by Cause, GFR category (G1 to G5) and Albuminuria category (A1 to A3), which is why it is called CGA staging. Risk of progression, cardiovascular events and death rises along both the GFR and the albuminuria axes. For the anaesthetist the stage guides drug choice, fluid and potassium management, and cardiac risk.

items: Abnormal kidney structure or function for >3 months
Marker 1: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² on its own is enough
Marker 2 (if eGFR is ≥60): albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g), urine sediment abnormality, electrolyte/tubular disorder, histology or imaging abnormality, or a kidney transplant
G1 and G2 count as CKD only if one of these other markers is present

rows: <15: kidney failure (G5D if on dialysis, G5T if transplant)
<30 mg/g (<3 mg/mmol): normal to mildly increased

items: Written as e.g. 'diabetic nephropathy, G3b A2'
Heat map: green (low risk), yellow, orange, red (very high risk)
A G2 patient with A3 can be at higher risk than a G3a patient with A1
Referral to a nephrologist usually from G4, or A3, or rapid fall in eGFR
RCRI: creatinine >2 mg/dL (177 µmol/L) is one risk factor
Muscle relaxant: cisatracurium or atracurium (Hofmann elimination)
Check K⁺ before suxamethonium (rises by ~0.5 mmol/L)
Morphine metabolites (M6G) build up; prefer fentanyl; avoid pethidine (norpethidine)
Sugammadex not recommended when CrCl <30
Dialysis patients: dialyse within 24 h before surgery, check post-dialysis weight and K⁺, protect the fistula arm
Avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxins; keep perfusion pressure up
Name the three axes: Cause, GFR, Albuminuria
Know the G3a/G3b split at 45
Know ACR cut-offs 30 and 300 mg/g (3 and 30 mg/mmol)
Uraemia: platelet dysfunction (consider desmopressin), anaemia, acidosis, delayed gastric emptying

items.pearl: Stage CKD on two axes: G by eGFR (90/60/45/30/15) and A by ACR (30/300).

refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of CKD

items.title: METs (functional capacity)
items.summary: A MET (metabolic equivalent) is the oxygen a person uses at rest, about 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min. Activities are rated in multiples of this to estimate functional capacity before surgery. Being able to do 4 METs or more (for example climbing a flight or two of stairs) usually means the patient can go ahead without further cardiac testing. Because clinicians' estimates are unreliable, structured tools such as DASI are now preferred.

items: 1 MET = resting O₂ consumption ≈ 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min (based on a 70 kg, 40-year-old man)
An activity of 4 METs uses about 4 times resting O₂

rows: Self-care, eating, dressing, walking indoors, slow walking on level ground, light housework
Climbing 1–2 flights of stairs, walking up a hill, brisk walking (~6 km/h), heavy housework like scrubbing floors

items: ACC/AHA: patient with elevated risk but ≥4 METs can usually proceed without stress testing
<4 METs or unknown, with elevated risk: consider further testing only if it would change management
ESC 2022: inability to climb 2 flights of stairs suggests poor capacity; DASI or NT-proBNP can refine risk
12-item questionnaire, score 0 to 58.2
Estimated VO₂peak = 0.43 × DASI + 9.6 (mL/kg/min); divide by 3.5 for METs
DASI >34 corresponds roughly to 4 METs and lower risk
METS study (Wijeysundera, Lancet 2018): subjective estimate of METs predicted outcomes poorly; DASI and NT-proBNP did better
CPET gold standard: anaerobic threshold <11 mL/kg/min and VO₂peak <15 suggest high risk for major surgery
Capacity may be limited by non-cardiac causes (arthritis, claudication), so it is then 'unknown'

items.pearl: Can climb two flights of stairs? That is about 4 METs, so usually no further cardiac testing.

refs.title: Wijeysundera DN et al. Assessment of functional capacity before major non-cardiac surgery (METS study). Lancet 2018

items.title: Body weight scalars & drug dosing (TBW vs IBW vs LBW vs ABW)
items.summary: In obesity, fat adds weight but adds little to cardiac output, blood volume or drug-clearing organs. So dosing everything by actual weight overdoses many drugs, while dosing by ideal weight underdoses some. Which weight to use depends on whether the drug spreads into fat (lipophilic), how it is cleared, and whether you are giving a single bolus or a maintenance infusion.

rows: What the scale says. Includes fat and lean tissue.
Male 50 + 0.91 x (height cm − 152.4); female 45.5 + 0.91 x (height cm − 152.4). Quick bedside: height cm − 100 (M) or − 105 (F).
Same as Devine IBW (ARDSnet). Used for tidal volume.
M: 9270 x TBW / (6680 + 216 x BMI); F: 9270 x TBW / (8780 + 244 x BMI). Plateaus around 100 kg (M) / 70 kg (F) however heavy the patient.
IBW + 0.4 x (TBW − IBW). Middle ground for drugs that partly distribute into fat.

items: Cardiac output and early drug distribution track lean mass, so induction bolus doses follow LBW.
Highly lipophilic drugs have a bigger volume of distribution in obesity, so repeated doses / infusions accumulate and need a larger weight (TBW or ABW) for maintenance.
Hydrophilic drugs (e.g. NMBAs) stay in lean tissue and ECF, so dose on IBW/LBW.
Clearance correlates best with LBW for most drugs.
Always titrate to effect; weight scalar is only the starting point.

rows: Induction: LBW. Maintenance infusion: TBW (or ABW); use BIS/pEEG.
Single bolus: TBW (big Vd); infusion: IBW (clearance not increased).
LBW (remifentanil infusion on TBW gives overdose and hypotension).
TBW, 1 to 1.5 mg/kg (plasma cholinesterase and ECF both increase).
IBW (LBW). Using TBW prolongs block. For RSI some give 1.2 mg/kg on LBW/ABW for faster onset.
Label: actual body weight (2 or 4 mg/kg; 16 mg/kg immediate). Studies suggest IBW + 40% is enough for moderate block.
TBW-based; prophylaxis often 40 mg BD if BMI > 40; treatment dose TBW, check anti-Xa if > 150 kg.

items: Classic rule: induction on LBW, maintenance on TBW (propofol); NMBAs on IBW; sux on TBW.
LBW is non-linear and plateaus; IBW ignores the extra lean mass that obese people do carry.
ABW correction factor is 0.4 (some sources use 0.3 or 0.5 for specific drugs).
PBW for ventilation — a favourite viva question in obese ARDS.
Mention monitoring: BIS/pEEG for TIVA, quantitative TOF for NMBAs, levels for antibiotics/heparin.

items.pearl: Bolus on lean, infuse on total; paralyse on ideal (except sux = total); ventilate on predicted.

items.title: Capnography waveforms (abnormal capnograms)
items.summary: A capnogram plots exhaled CO₂ against time for each breath. The shape tells you more than the EtCO₂ number: where the tube is, whether the airway is narrowed, whether the circuit is leaking or letting you rebreathe, and whether the heart is pumping blood through the lungs. Read it in order: baseline, upstroke, plateau, downstroke, then the trend over many breaths.

sections.alt: Normal capnogram with phases 0, I, II and III, alpha and beta angles
rows: Baseline: dead-space gas with no CO₂. Should sit at zero.
Steep upstroke: mixing of dead-space and alveolar gas.
Alveolar plateau, gently rising. EtCO₂ is read at its end.
Inspiratory downstroke back to zero (some texts call it phase IV).
Between II and III, normally about 100–110°. Wider = airway obstruction.
Between III and 0, normally about 90°. Wider = rebreathing.
35–45 mmHg; usually 2–5 mmHg below PaCO₂ in healthy lungs.
Slow, sloping upstroke and steep phase III: the 'shark fin'. Wide α angle.
A dip in the plateau: the patient is making small breaths against the ventilator as relaxant wears off. Surgeons leaning on the chest or abdomen can mimic it.
Small, rounded waves with a poorly defined plateau.
Tall mandatory breaths mixed with smaller spontaneous ones; comparing their heights shows how much the patient is doing.
Small ripples on the end of the plateau or downstroke during a long expiratory pause, from the heartbeat moving gas at the sensor. Harmless.
sections.tip: Tap a pattern to see its waveform.

rows: Baseline does not return to zero: exhausted soda lime, faulty valves, or low fresh gas flow in a Mapleson circuit.
Exhaled gas is re-inhaled from the expiratory limb: raised baseline and a slurred inspiratory downstroke.
Exhaled gas passes back into the inspiratory limb and is re-inhaled: slanted downstroke, baseline may not reach zero.
Rebreathing dip and raised baseline are expected if fresh gas flow is too low for the minute ventilation.
Sudden step-up of baseline and EtCO₂ from secretions or water in the sampling line or sensor.
Air dilutes the sample: low EtCO₂ and an odd double-peaked plateau (sidestream monitors).
A few small, shrinking waves (CO₂ washed out of the stomach) that fall to zero within about 6 breaths.
Disconnection, extubation, blocked tube or sampling line, or cardiac arrest. Check the patient first.

<svg viewBox="0 0 240 80" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" focusable="false" aria-hidden="true"><line x1="4" y1="69" x2="236" y2="69" class="nf-l"/><path d="M4,68 L20,68 L26,20 L66,18 L71,68 L71,68 L87,68 L93,20 L133,18 L138,68 L236,68" class="nf-p"/></svg>
Waves appear with each compression. EtCO₂ <10 mmHg suggests poor compressions; a sudden rise to normal levels suggests return of circulation.
Fall in cardiac output or pulmonary blood flow: massive PE, air embolism, severe hypotension.
EtCO₂ climbs breath after breath with a normal zero baseline (soda lime still absorbing). Often the earliest sign.
Normal phase II but steeper phase III; a normal variant. EtCO₂ can equal or exceed PaCO₂.
Two peaks in phase III: the first from the new healthy lung, the second from the slow-emptying native lung.

items: Six breaths of a sustained, regular capnogram is the gold standard for confirming tracheal intubation.
A capnogram can be present in an oesophageal intubation for the first few breaths (gastric CO₂ after bag-mask ventilation or carbonated drinks), then it fades.
Shark fin = obstruction (bronchospasm, kinked tube, COPD). Raised baseline = rebreathing.
Gradual rise in EtCO₂ with normal baseline: think MH, hypoventilation, fever, laparoscopic CO₂ absorption, tourniquet or clamp release.
Sudden fall: think circuit first (disconnection, leak), then circulation (arrest, embolism).
During CPR, EtCO₂ guides compression quality and is often the first sign of ROSC.

items.pearl: Read the shape before the number: zero baseline, square plateau, steady trend. A shark fin means obstruction, a lifted baseline means rebreathing.

items.title: AP vs PA chest X-ray
items.summary: The letters say which way the X-ray beam travels. In a PA film the beam goes from back to front with the chest pressed against the detector; in an AP film it goes front to back, usually on a portable machine with the patient sitting or supine in bed. PA is the standard because it shows the heart and mediastinum close to true size. Most ICU and post-op films are AP, so you must adjust how you read them.

rows: Standing, front of chest against the detector, chin up, hands on hips and shoulders rolled forward. Tube about 180 cm (72 in) away. Full inspiration.
Beam from the front, detector behind the back. Sitting or supine, often portable. Tube closer, about 100 cm (40 in). Inspiration often poorer.
Viewed the same way: as if facing the patient, heart on the image's right side.

sections.h: Why the heart looks bigger on AP
items: The heart lies anteriorly, so on AP it is farther from the detector and gets magnified.
The shorter tube distance makes the beam more divergent, adding more magnification.
Poorer inspiration and the supine position make the heart and upper mediastinum look wider still.
Rule: CTR >0.5 means cardiomegaly only on a good PA film. Do not diagnose cardiomegaly from CTR on AP alone; a normal-looking heart on AP is reassuring.

sections.h: How to tell them apart on the film
rows: AP films are usually marked AP / portable / supine / erect. Check the label first.
PA: rotated off the lung fields. AP: overlie the upper lateral lungs.
AP: higher and more horizontal, projected over or above the apices. PA: lower, more V-shaped.
AP: heart and superior mediastinum look larger and wider.
PA usually shows more posterior ribs above the diaphragm; AP often fewer (poorer inflation).
An air-fluid level in the stomach means the patient was upright (PA or erect AP).

items: Pleural fluid layers behind the lung: a diffuse haze over one side instead of a blunted costophrenic angle and meniscus.
Pneumothorax air collects anteriorly and at the bases: look for a deep, lucent costophrenic sulcus (deep sulcus sign) rather than an apical rim.
Upper lobe vessels look as large as lower lobe vessels when supine; this is normal, not upper lobe diversion.
Free air under the diaphragm and air-fluid levels need an erect (or decubitus) film.
Mediastinal widening may be just projection; compare with old films and the clinical picture.
ICU and ward portable films, trauma bay, post-op recovery, anyone who cannot stand.
Checking ETT tip, central line, NG tube, chest drain position and pneumothorax after a line.
Comparing serial ICU films is best done on films taken the same way (same projection and position).
PA is the standard view; AP is a compromise for sick or immobile patients.
Two reasons for AP magnification: heart far from detector and short tube distance with divergent beam.
CTR >0.5 = cardiomegaly only on PA.
Quick tells for AP: label, scapulae over lungs, high horizontal clavicles.
Supine film: effusion = haze, pneumothorax = deep sulcus sign, no fluid levels.

items.pearl: Never call cardiomegaly on an AP film: the heart is magnified because it is far from the detector and the tube is close.

items.title: Paediatric epidural dosing (bolus & infusion)
items.summary: Epidurals in children are dosed by weight, and for a catheter by how many dermatomes you need to cover. You give a loading bolus of dilute local anaesthetic, then a low-concentration infusion with a strict mg/kg/hr ceiling. Neonates get about half the older-child infusion rate because they clear amide local anaesthetics slowly. Dilute solutions are the rule: 0.5% bupivacaine or ropivacaine is rarely needed.

rows: 0.05 mL/kg per dermatome to be covered from the catheter tip
About 0.5 mL/kg of 0.25% bupivacaine is a practical starting load
Bolus up to 1 mL/kg, maximum 20 mL
Epinephrine-containing test dose first; watch for a rise in T wave, HR or BP
0.4 mg/kg/hr (some centres up to 0.5 mg/kg/hr maximum)
0.2 mg/kg/hr in neonates/infants, 0.4 mg/kg/hr in older children, ideally no longer than 48 h

items: Fentanyl: 1–2 mcg/kg bolus, or about 2 mcg/mL added to the infusion
Clonidine: about 2 mcg/kg bolus or 0.1 mcg/kg/hr infusion; can cause sedation, bradycardia and hypotension, and apnoea in neonates
Epinephrine 1:200,000 in the test dose and to prolong a single shot
Avoid epidural opioids or use them cautiously in neonates and ex-prems unless monitored (respiratory depression)
Low alpha-1 acid glycoprotein: more free (active) local anaesthetic in the blood
Immature liver enzymes: amides accumulate during a long infusion, so halve the rate and limit duration
Relatively higher cardiac output: faster systemic absorption of the bolus
Conus at about L3 and dura at about S3–S4 in infants: placement is lower and caudal-threaded catheters are common
Epidural depth in children is roughly 1 mm/kg (or 0.1 cm/kg)
Know the three numbers: 2.5 mg/kg bupivacaine single shot, 0.2 mg/kg/hr neonate infusion, 0.4 mg/kg/hr older child
Worked example, 10 kg child: 5 mL 0.25% bupivacaine (12.5 mg, well under 25 mg), then 0.1% at 3 mL/hr
Children under about 8 years rarely get hypotension from a sympathetic block (immature sympathetic tone)
Toxicity under GA may show only as arrhythmia or cardiovascular collapse; know the lipid emulsion dose (20% at 1.5 mL/kg)
Always check your hospital's protocol: rates vary between centres

items.pearl: Neonate 0.2, child 0.4 mg/kg/hr; bolus 0.05 mL/kg per dermatome; never above 2.5 mg/kg bupivacaine.

items.title: Bone cement implantation syndrome (BCIS)
items.summary: BCIS is sudden hypoxia, hypotension, arrhythmia, loss of consciousness or cardiac arrest around the time of cementing in arthroplasty, most often cemented hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture. Pressurised cement pushes marrow, fat, cement and air into the venous circulation; the emboli plus mediator release raise pulmonary vascular resistance and the right ventricle fails. It is a major cause of intraoperative death in frail elderly hip-fracture patients, so prevention and vigilance at cementation matter most.

items: Cementation, prosthesis insertion or joint reduction (within minutes)
Occasionally at tourniquet deflation in cemented knee replacement
Also seen in other cemented procedures (vertebroplasty, shoulder)

rows: SpO2 < 88% or SBP falls > 40% or unexpected loss of consciousness (regional)

items: Embolic model (favoured): high intramedullary pressure → fat, marrow, cement and air emboli → raised PVR → acute RV failure → low output
Echo shows emboli 'snowstorm' in right heart at cementing
Mediators: histamine, complement activation, anaphylactoid picture
Methyl methacrylate monomer vasodilation: probably minor at clinical levels
Final pathway: RV ischaemia, hypotension, hypoxia (V/Q mismatch), arrest
ASA III–IV, frail elderly
Pre-existing pulmonary hypertension, significant cardiac disease, RV dysfunction
COPD, diuretic use, male sex
Pathological fracture/metastases, osteoporosis, intertrochanteric fracture
Long-stem femoral prosthesis, unreamed canal
Identify high-risk patients preop; discuss cemented vs uncemented with surgeon
Surgeon tells anaesthetist before cementing; anaesthetist watches closely
Surgical: medullary lavage, good haemostasis, venting, retrograde cement gun, gentle pressurisation in high risk
Anaesthetic: euvolaemia before cementing, raise FiO2, invasive BP in high risk, vasopressor drawn up
Avoid nitrous oxide (air emboli)
100% oxygen; secure airway if needed
Fluids to support RV preload (cautiously)
Vasopressor: phenylephrine/noradrenaline to keep coronary perfusion of the RV; adrenaline if severe
Inotropes for RV failure; consider pulmonary vasodilators in ICU
Grade 3: ALS/CPR; post-event ICU and echo
Know the 3 Donaldson grades with numbers
Embolic → raised PVR → RV failure is the key mechanism
AAGBI 2015 guideline: three-way team roles (surgeon, anaesthetist, team) at cementation
Grades 2–3 carry markedly higher 30-day mortality
Treatment is supportive: O2, fluids, alpha agonist, inotrope, CPR

items.pearl: Cementing = embolic hit to the right heart: 100% O2, fill, and an alpha agonist ready before the surgeon pressurises.

items.title: Opioid receptors (mu, delta, kappa, NOP)
items.summary: Opioids act on four related receptors: mu (MOP), delta (DOP), kappa (KOP) and the nociceptin receptor (NOP, also called ORL-1). All are inhibitory G-protein (Gi/o) coupled receptors found in the brain, spinal cord dorsal horn and periphery (gut). Mu is the one that matters most clinically: it gives the analgesia we want and most of the side effects we fear, especially respiratory depression. Kappa gives spinal analgesia and sedation with dysphoria, and naloxone blocks mu, delta and kappa but not NOP.

items: Gi/o coupled: inhibit adenylyl cyclase → less cAMP
Open K⁺ channels → neuron hyperpolarises (postsynaptic inhibition)
Close voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → less transmitter release (presynaptic inhibition, e.g. less substance P and glutamate in dorsal horn)
Net effect: pain signals damped at spinal (substantia gelatinosa) and supraspinal (PAG, rostral ventromedial medulla) levels; descending inhibition is switched on

rows: Mu – guinea pig ileum · Delta – mouse vas deferens · Kappa – rabbit vas deferens
Mu – β-endorphin, endomorphins · Delta – leu- and met-enkephalin · Kappa – dynorphin · NOP – nociceptin/orphanin FQ
Mu – morphine, fentanyl · Delta – deltorphin · Kappa – pentazocine (table also lists buprenorphine, see caution below)
Naloxone for all three (highest affinity for mu; kappa needs bigger doses). NOP is naloxone-insensitive
Supraspinal and spinal: yes for all three
Mu yes; delta and kappa no (per table)
Mu yes, kappa yes, delta no
Mu yes, kappa yes, delta no

Analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression, miosis, bradycardia, constipation, nausea/vomiting, pruritus, urinary retention, tolerance and physical dependence. Old split: μ1 analgesia, μ2 respiratory depression/GI – not confirmed by cloning (one gene)
Spinal analgesia, sedation, dysphoria/psychotomimetic effects, diuresis (ADH inhibition), miosis, less respiratory depression – a 'ceiling' effect
Analgesia (mainly spinal), modulates mu activity; no clinically used selective agonist
Fourth member, ~60% similar structure; spinal analgesia but supraspinal anti-opioid effect; not reversed by naloxone; buprenorphine has some NOP action

items: Buprenorphine is really a mu PARTIAL agonist with very high mu affinity and slow dissociation, and a kappa ANTAGONIST – it is listed under kappa agonists in the table, but quote it as a mu partial agonist in the viva
Pentazocine (and butorphanol, nalbuphine) are kappa agonist–mu antagonist/partial agonists: can precipitate withdrawal in mu-dependent patients
Delta 'no respiratory depression' is from older animal work; delta agonists may add to mu depression
Naloxone is non-selective but best at mu – high-dose buprenorphine respiratory depression is hard to reverse (needs large doses/infusion)
IUPHAR names: MOP, DOP, KOP, NOP (old: OP3, OP1, OP2, ORL-1)
All 7-transmembrane Gi/o GPCRs: ↓cAMP, ↑K⁺ conductance, ↓Ca²⁺ entry
Remember bioassays: Guinea pig → mu, Mouse → delta, Rabbit → kappa
Ligands: Endorphin–mu, Enkephalin–delta, Dynorphin–kappa (E-E-D in order mu-delta-kappa)
Respiratory depression is a mu effect – blunted CO₂ response at brainstem
Kappa = dysphoria + diuresis + spinal analgesia with ceiling on respiratory depression
Naloxone does not block NOP

items.pearl: Mu does everything (good and bad); kappa = sedation, dysphoria, diuresis; and buprenorphine is a mu partial agonist / kappa antagonist despite the table.

items.title: Tourniquet in ortho procedures – anaesthetic implications
items.summary: A pneumatic tourniquet gives a bloodless field for limb surgery, but it makes the limb ischaemic and compresses the tissue under the cuff. Inflation adds volume and afterload to the circulation; after 30–60 min tourniquet pain pushes up HR and BP; deflation releases cold, acidic, CO2- and potassium-rich blood and drops the BP. The anaesthetist has to anticipate each of these phases and watch for local injury.

rows: Ideally limb occlusion pressure (LOP) + a safety margin (≈ +40 mmHg if LOP < 130, +60 if 131–190, +80 if > 190). Older rule of thumb: SBP + 50–75 mmHg (arm) and SBP + 100–150 mmHg (thigh).
Often ~250 mmHg arm and ~300 mmHg leg; higher pressure = more nerve/muscle injury, so use the lowest that works and a wide cuff.
Aim ≤ 2 h continuous (many use 1.5–2 h); warn the surgeon at 1 h and at intervals. If longer is needed, deflate for a reperfusion break (about 10–15 min) before re-inflating.
Pressure, inflation and deflation times, site, and who applied it – a gauge must be used with pneumatic cuffs.

items: Exsanguination (Esmarch / elevation) shifts blood into the central circulation: ≈ 15% of blood volume for both legs (up to ~800 mL); much less for one arm.
Transient rise in CVP and BP; raised afterload – can tip patients with poor LV function, AS/MS or fluid overload into failure. Avoid bilateral simultaneous exsanguination in them.
Limb becomes ischaemic: within the limb, lactate, K+ and CO2 rise and pH falls; cellular ATP runs low by about 2–3 h.
Slight core temperature rise (less heat loss from the excluded limb), more noticeable in children.
Hypercoagulable state during inflation (catecholamine surge, venous stasis).
Starts about 30–60 min after inflation, even under GA (rising HR/BP) or a working spinal (dull, poorly localised ache).
Thought to be carried by small unmyelinated C fibres, which are relatively spared by the block; once the larger A-delta fibres are blocked by ischaemia, C-fibre pain comes through.
Settles quickly after deflation.

Prevention/treatment: dense block (higher dose / intrathecal opioid, clonidine or dexmedetomidine adjuncts), deepen GA, opioids, ketamine (small dose, e.g. 0.25 mg/kg), magnesium; tourniquet cuff below the level of the block – EMLA under the cuff for IVRA.
Difficult hypertension that does not respond often only goes on deflation – tell the surgeon about timing.

BP falls (reduced afterload, blood pooling into the reactive hyperaemic limb, washout of vasodilating metabolites) – more with leg tourniquets and in the volume-depleted; give fluid/vasopressor and stagger bilateral deflations.
EtCO2 rises, peaking around 1 min and lasting ~10 min; spontaneously breathing patients increase minute ventilation; ventilated patients need minute ventilation raised.
Increased CBF from the CO2 rise – a problem in head injury/raised ICP (common in polytrauma); hyperventilate shortly before deflation.
Transient metabolic acidosis, small rise in K+ (≈ 0.3 mmol/L after 1–2 h) and lactate; a bigger issue with long tourniquet times, bilateral release or renal failure.
Core temperature drops by ~0.5–0.8 °C as cold limb blood returns – keep the patient warm.
Brief fibrinolysis after release and showers of emboli (fat, thrombus, cement) – PE and paradoxical embolism risk; watch for BCIS in cemented arthroplasty.
Remember LA / IVRA: in a Bier block do not deflate before 20 min, and ideally stage the release, to avoid LA toxicity.
Nerve injury (radial most common in the arm, then sciatic/peroneal in the leg) – usually from high pressure at the cuff edge; mostly neurapraxia.
Muscle injury, post-tourniquet syndrome (swollen, stiff, weak limb), compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis with long times.
Skin: pressure sores, friction blisters, chemical burns from prep pooling under the cuff – use padding and keep prep out.
Masks ischaemia or bleeding until release – check haemostasis after deflation.

Relative contraindications: peripheral vascular disease or bypass graft in the limb, previous DVT in that limb, sickle cell disease (relative), severe crush injury, poor skin, infection or tumour distal (exsanguination by elevation only).
Say the three phases: inflation (volume + afterload), maintenance (pain/hypertension at 30–60 min, ischaemia), deflation (hypotension, ↑EtCO2, ↓pH, ↑K+, ↓temp, emboli).
Pressure: LOP-based is best; quote SBP + 50–75 (arm) / + 100–150 (thigh) as the classic rule; time ≤ 2 h.
Why tourniquet pain breaks through a spinal: C fibres and their relative block resistance – manage with a denser block or adjuncts.
Before release in a head-injured patient: increase minute ventilation and have fluids/pressor ready.
Antibiotic prophylaxis must be given before inflation (ideally ≥ 5 min before) – otherwise it never reaches the operative site.
Sickle cell disease and PVD are the classic relative contraindications to quote.

items.pearl: Give the antibiotic before the cuff goes up, and turn the ventilator up before the cuff comes down.

items.title: ECG normal values, intervals & QTc
items.summary: The numbers every ECG reading starts with: paper speed, box sizes, and the normal PR, QRS and QT. Most criteria in the other ECG notes are just these numbers pushed out of range.

rows: 1 mm = 40 ms across, 0.1 mV up (at 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV)
300 ÷ large boxes between two R waves (or 1500 ÷ small boxes)
QRS count on a 10 s strip × 6
120–200 ms. Short (< 120): pre-excitation (WPW). Long (> 200): first-degree AV block
60–100 ms. 100–120: incomplete BBB / non-specific delay. ≥ 120: complete BBB, VT, hyperkalaemia, paced
Abnormal above 440 ms in men and 460 ms in women (ESC cut-offs)
P before every QRS; P upright in I and II, negative in aVR

items: Bazett: QTc = QT ÷ √(RR in seconds)
Bazett over-corrects at fast rates and under-corrects at slow rates
Measure QT in II or V5, from QRS onset to the end of the T wave; leave out a separate U wave
Count PR in small boxes: more than 5 = first-degree block; fewer than 3 = short PR
QRS of 3 small boxes or more = broad
Long QT + bradycardia + low K⁺/Mg²⁺ + QT drugs = torsades risk under anaesthesia

items.pearl: Five small boxes = one large box = 200 ms = 1 second ÷ 5.

items.title: Stewart (strong ion) approach & base excess partitioning
items.summary: Stewart says pH is set by three independent things: PaCO₂, the strong ion difference (mainly Na⁺ minus Cl⁻) and weak acids (mainly albumin). Bicarbonate just follows. The bedside version splits the base excess into a chloride part, an albumin part and the unmeasured-anion remainder.

rows: Na⁺ + K⁺ + Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺ − Cl⁻ − lactate; normal about +40. A lower SID = acidosis
Mainly albumin (about 78%) and phosphate. Low albumin = alkalosis
HCO₃⁻ + charge on albumin and phosphate
SIDa − SIDe; normal about 0. Raised = unmeasured anions (ketones, toxins, renal acids)
Na⁺ − Cl⁻ − 38 (newer versions use 35 or 32). Negative = hyperchloraemic acidosis
Base excess − (Na–Cl effect + albumin effect + lactate effect)

items: After 6 L saline: BE −10, Na 140, Cl 115, albumin 30 g/L, lactate 2
Na–Cl effect: 140 − 115 − 38 = −13 (acidifying)
Albumin effect: 0.25 × (42 − 30) = +3 (alkalinising)
Lactate effect: −2
Unmeasured anions: −10 − (−13 + 3 − 2) = +2, i.e. essentially none: the acidosis is the chloride

Why saline acidifies: it has an SID of 0 (Na 154, Cl 154), so large volumes dilute the plasma SID; balanced fluids contain metabolisable anions (lactate, acetate, gluconate) that leave a higher effective SID
Hypoalbuminaemia is a metabolic alkalosis in Stewart terms and can hide an acidosis
Both approaches describe the same blood; Stewart explains WHY (chloride, albumin, unmeasured ions)

items.pearl: Na − Cl tells the chloride story; albumin is a weak acid; what is left is unmeasured anions.

items.summary: Practical points behind the numbers: when a venous gas is good enough, how a bad sample changes the result, how to read lactate, and how temperature changes blood gases on bypass.

rows: Venous about 0.03–0.04 lower; good agreement, acceptable for most decisions
Venous about 5–6 mmHg higher on average, but wide spread; a normal venous PCO₂ makes arterial hypercapnia unlikely
Venous PO₂ cannot replace arterial; use SpO₂ or an ABG
PO₂ moves towards room air (rises on air, can fall if the patient is on high O₂); PCO₂ falls
Cells keep metabolising: PO₂ and glucose fall, PCO₂ and lactate rise (worse with very high white counts)
Dilutes the sample: falsely low PCO₂ and HCO₃⁻
Low PO₂ that does not fit the SpO₂

items: Normal under 2 mmol/L; ≥ 4 in sepsis marks high risk
Type A: poor tissue oxygen delivery (shock, hypoxia, severe anaemia, ischaemic gut)
Type B: no hypoperfusion (metformin, liver failure, adrenaline/salbutamol, thiamine deficiency, malignancy)
Lactate clearance over hours is a useful guide in resuscitation

rows: Gases dissolve more, so measured partial pressures fall and pH rises
Gases read at 37 °C and kept normal at 37 °C; protein charge (histidine "alpha") stays constant; keeps cerebral autoregulation; used in most adults
Gases corrected to the actual cold temperature and kept normal, which needs added CO₂; more cerebral blood flow; often used for deep hypothermia in children

items: Analysers measure at 37 °C; "temperature-corrected" values are calculated
Expel all air within 2 minutes and run the sample within about 10 minutes, or keep it on crushed ice (PO₂ fell within 20 min at room temperature in Biswas 1982)
A VBG is fine for DKA follow-up; get an ABG when you need PaO₂ or an accurate PaCO₂ in shock

items.summary: One order to read every gas, then six fully worked examples covering the patterns most likely in the exam and in theatre. Each answer was calculated with the same rules as the other ABG notes.

Oxygenation: PaO₂ for the FiO₂, A–a gradient or P/F

pH 7.53, PaCO₂ 47, HCO₃⁻ 38, Cl 86 → metabolic alkalosis; expected 46.6 ± 5: appropriate; low Cl⁻ → chloride-responsive: give saline + K⁺
pH 7.35, PaCO₂ 60, HCO₃⁻ 32 → respiratory acidosis; chronic prediction 32 → chronic, compensated: his baseline

pH 7.35, PaCO₂ 32, HCO₃⁻ 17, Na 141, Cl 113 → metabolic acidosis; Winter's 33.5 ± 2: appropriate; AG 11 → hyperchloraemic NAGMA

items.title: Pregnancy physiology (1/2): CVS, respiratory & airway
items.summary: Pregnancy drives the heart and lungs harder to meet a ~20% (rising to ~60% in labour) increase in oxygen demand. The heart pumps more into a dilated, low-resistance circulation, while the lungs breathe more against a smaller FRC. For the anaesthetist this means supine hypotension, fast desaturation, a harder airway and a mother who tolerates blood loss well until she suddenly doesn't.

rows: ↑ 40–50% (HR ↑ 15–25%, SV ↑ 20–30%); rises a further ~40% in labour and peaks up to ~80% above pre-labour immediately after delivery (autotransfusion)
↓ 20–30% from ~8 weeks (progesterone, oestrogen, NO, low-resistance placental bed)
Diastolic falls more than systolic; nadir mid-trimester, back to baseline by term
Unchanged despite bigger blood volume (vessels and ventricles dilate)
Displaced up and left – left axis deviation on ECG, flow murmur and S3 can be normal; mild LV hypertrophy

items: From ~20 weeks the supine uterus compresses the IVC (↓ preload, CO can fall ~25%) and the aorta (↓ uterine perfusion).
Supine hypotensive syndrome: hypotension, pallor, sweating, nausea, bradycardia in some; can be concealed – fetal distress may be the first sign.
Prevent: left lateral tilt ~15° or manual left uterine displacement for every supine parturient >20 weeks, including during CPR.
Worse after neuraxial or GA, because the sympathetic compensation (vasoconstriction of lower limbs) is lost.

rows: ↑ ~20% at term, up to ~60% in labour
↑ 45–50% – mainly from tidal volume (↑ ~40%); RR changes little. Progesterone drives this
↓ ~20% (diaphragm pushed up ~4 cm); may fall below closing capacity when supine → airway closure, shunt
PaCO₂ ~30 mmHg (4 kPa), HCO₃⁻ ~20 mmol/L, pH ~7.44 – compensated respiratory alkalosis; PaO₂ slightly ↑
FEV₁, FEV₁/FVC, vital capacity, compliance of lung (chest wall compliance ↓)
Rises (~30 mmHg) → right shift helps O₂ unloading to the fetus

items: Capillary engorgement and oedema of nasal/oral mucosa and larynx (worse in pre-eclampsia and after prolonged pushing): use a smaller tube (6.0–7.0 mm), avoid nasal instrumentation (bleeding).
Breast enlargement and weight gain make laryngoscopy harder – use a short handle, ramp (head-elevated laryngoscopy position).
Failed tracheal intubation is roughly 1 in 390 obstetric GAs (≈8× general surgical); follow OAA/DAS obstetric difficult airway guideline.
Rapid desaturation at apnoea (↓FRC + ↑O₂ use): preoxygenate to EtO₂ ≥0.9, consider high-flow nasal O₂ and head-up.
Faster inhalational induction (↑ minute ventilation, ↓FRC) and MAC ↓ up to ~30%.
Lower PaCO₂ is the normal target under ventilation (~30–32 mmHg); hyperventilation below this causes uterine vasoconstriction and left-shifts maternal Hb.
CO rise is the reason high-risk cardiac lesions (MS, AS, pulmonary hypertension) decompensate – watch the 2nd trimester, labour and the immediate post-partum period.
Signs of hypovolaemia appear late: up to ~1000–1500 mL loss before tachycardia/hypotension.
Normal pregnancy ABG: PaCO₂ 30, HCO₃⁻ 20, pH 7.44 – a 'normal' PaCO₂ of 40 in a parturient is relative hypercapnia.
CO returns towards baseline over ~2 weeks and is near normal by 6 weeks; respiratory changes by 6–8 weeks post-partum.

items.pearl: Tilt left, pre-oxygenate well, small tube – the parturient desaturates fast and is harder to intubate.

items.title: Pregnancy physiology (2/2): blood, GI, renal, CNS & drugs
items.summary: Pregnancy expands the plasma more than the red cells (dilutional anaemia), makes the blood hypercoagulable, loosens the gastro-oesophageal barrier and increases kidney filtration. Hormones and engorged epidural veins also make the mother more sensitive to anaesthetic drugs. These changes explain aspiration risk, VTE prophylaxis, reduced spinal/epidural doses and lower MAC.

rows: ↑ 40–50%; red cell mass ↑ only 20–30% → dilutional (physiological) anaemia, Hb ~110–120 g/L
↑ ~35–45% (≈ +1–1.5 L) – prepares for delivery blood loss
↑ fibrinogen (~4–6 g/L at term), VII, VIII, X, XII, vWF; ↓ XI, XIII, protein S; ↓ fibrinolysis → hypercoagulable
Neutrophilia, up to ~15 ×10⁹/L, higher in labour
Several-fold higher, highest in the first weeks post-partum

items: Progesterone relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter; the uterus pushes the stomach up and changes the angle of the GO junction → reflux, heartburn.
Gastric emptying is normal in pregnancy but slows in labour, especially with systemic opioids.
Treat as 'full stomach' from about 18–20 weeks and in labour: antacid prophylaxis (H₂ blocker / PPI ± sodium citrate, metoclopramide) and RSI for GA.
Liver: albumin falls (↓ oncotic pressure, ↑ free fraction of bound drugs); ALP rises from placenta – normal; transaminases and bilirubin should stay normal.

rows: Fall (creatinine ~45–70 µmol/L) – a 'normal' non-pregnant value may mean renal impairment
Glycosuria and mild proteinuria (<300 mg/day) can be normal; ureters and pelvis dilate (R > L) → UTI risk

items: MAC of volatile agents reduced by up to ~30% (progesterone, endorphins).
Neuraxial local anaesthetic requirement ↓ ~25–30%: engorged epidural veins reduce epidural/CSF space volume, lumbar lordosis aids cephalad spread and nerves are more sensitive.
Plasma cholinesterase ↓ ~25% – suxamethonium action barely prolonged clinically.
Thyroid: total T3/T4 ↑ with TBG, free levels normal. Insulin resistance in the 2nd/3rd trimester (gestational diabetes).
Larger volume of distribution and ↑ clearance alter drug levels; ionised (basic) drugs can 'trap' in the more acidic fetus (e.g. local anaesthetics in fetal acidosis).
Hypercoagulability is protective at delivery but makes VTE a leading cause of maternal death – think LMWH timing before neuraxial (12 h prophylactic, 24 h treatment dose).
Spinal dose is lower in the term parturient; volume/height matter less than in non-pregnant spinals.
Pregnancy itself is ASA II.
Recovery times post-partum: coagulation ~2 weeks (risk 6 weeks), renal ~4–6 weeks, GI changes within 1–2 days (but treat as full stomach for ~24–48 h).

items.pearl: Lower MAC, lower spinal dose, full stomach from ~20 weeks, and a clot-prone patient until 6 weeks post-partum.
